title: Hearing every tune in two veins, Armstrong's and Coleman Hawkins's
summary: Randolph says he hears tunes in both a Louis vein and a Hawkins vein and teaches this idiom to pupils.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: So, I said, 'That's the kind of horn I want to play, I want to play that.' That's a funny thing about my playing and my hearing of tunes. Whenever I hear a tune, I hear it in two veins. I hear in Louie vein and a Coleman Hawkins vein. And I can duplicate either one for you on the paper.
Uh-huh. Louie's very lyrical, Hawk is very vertical (very vocal) -- harmonic player.
Now you take Hawkins -- and I have some

of my pupils sometimes doing the same thing. And I try to hum it to give them the idiom, you know. That idiom that Hawkins for instance, if Hawkins, does with that -- (unintelligible) if he's going to pay a number like -- let's just say "Don't Blame Me" (unintelligible) like dum-dum-da-da- -- Hawkins would say -- do-do-do-do- Well, I write that kind of thing. See, and I try to give it to them. And the trumpet's the same way. But sometimes you can -- well, it's like that old mule I used to plow when I was a boy. I used to think because I was really thirsty, the mule was thirsty and I would try to make him drink. I couldn't make him drink.
Lead a horse to water, right.
